interest: This file offers a concise administrative window into the intersection of intellectual property disputes, international trade tensions, and pre-World War II Japanese industrial policy during the 1930s. It vividly illustrates the challenges faced by American manufacturers—from specialized firms producing tubular watch straps or lithographic presses to multinationals like Singer—confronting aggressive Japanese reverse-engineering, trademark infringement, and state-favored patent appropriation. Particularly striking are entries revealing that the Japanese Legation in Lisbon actively circulated marketing materials for unauthorized copycat parts bearing Singer's 'SIMANCO' trademark, as well as the progression toward 1938–1939 wartime exchange and import controls that severely restricted foreign business operations and trapped corporate earnings in Japan. Furthermore, the records demonstrate the State Department's strict legalistic doctrine of declining diplomatic intervention where claimants lacked a local domicile under Japan's Unfair Competition Law or had not exhausted domestic legal remedies.
overview: This file comprises State Department 'List of Papers' docket sheets for decimal file 894.542, spanning from 1930 to 1939, recording official correspondence, legal memoranda, and cross-references regarding patents, patent infringements, and industrial property rights in Japan. The documents trace complaints brought by American firms and inventors—including General Printing Ink Corporation, General Reduction Corporation, Pridwin Industries, Prophylactic Toothbrush Company, A. Sauer and Company, and Singer Manufacturing Company—concerning unauthorized duplication of American machinery, tools, and consumer goods by Japanese competitors, as well as Japanese legislative developments such as the Unfair Competition Law of 1934 and the 1938 Patent Law revision. Throughout these cases, the State Department consistently maintained that it lacked authority to intervene diplomatically without clear treaty violations or local branch establishment under Japanese law, advising aggrieved American businesses to retain private local counsel or pursue domestic legal remedies such as customs exclusions and federal court injunctions.

subfiles.about: Docket register sheets recording correspondence and cross-references regarding Japanese patent legislation, unfair competition laws, and inquiries concerning protection for American inventions between 1933 and 1938.
subfiles.summary: This three-page docket sheet indexes documents filed under main decimal file 894.542 from July 1933 to July 1938. It records inquiries by Senator Robert J. Bulkley regarding Japanese plant visits to General Tire & Rubber Co., reports from Consul General Arthur Garrels in Tokyo on Japan's Unfair Competition Law (Law No. 14 of 1934), and cross-references concerning ore-smelting inventions, TVA inquiries, and diesel engines. In addition, it details patent infringement complaints from Albert White (hooked rug machines), licensing questions from Prescott W. Cookingham (Phillips Screw Company), purchase proposals from Mrs. M. P. Cabell (Foreign Refinoil Company), and Ambassador Joseph C. Grew's transmission of the revised Japanese Patent Law (Law No. 3 of 1938).
subfiles.title: Department of State List of Papers: Patents — Japan (894.542/6 to 894.542/16)

subfiles.about: Docket sheet summarizing the 1930 case regarding alleged infringement of General Printing Ink Corporation's machinery patents by Japanese companies in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: This docket sheet summarizes correspondence from January and February 1930 concerning patent infringement protests filed by the General Printing Ink Corporation. The company reported that Hoshima Lithographing Co. and Tokyo Teikan Kaisha, Ltd., both of Tokyo, had secured Japanese patents duplicating its Phoenix Type 'F' Rapid Drying Lithograph oven and Improved Rutherford Rotary Metal Decorating Press. The Department of State informed the firm that no diplomatic intervention was possible under the 1911 Industrial Property Convention and relevant Japanese law, offering instead to furnish contact information for private legal counsel in Japan.
subfiles.title: Department of State List of Papers: Patent of General Printing Ink Corporation in Japan

subfiles.about: Docket sheet recording the 1931 case concerning the Japanese government's refusal to grant metallurgical patents to the General Reduction Corporation.
subfiles.summary: This docket sheet covers correspondence from April 1931 submitted by patent attorneys Prindle, Bean and Mann on behalf of the General Reduction Corporation and its president, William H. Smith. The attorneys requested diplomatic protests after the Japanese government rejected patent applications for two corporate inventions. Following the State Department's request for further details regarding the legal standing of the applications before deciding whether to take up the case, the attorneys formally withdrew the petition, stating that their clients had determined the patents were not worth contesting.
subfiles.title: Department of State List of Papers: Protection of Patent Rights of General Reduction Corporation in Japan

subfiles.about: Docket sheet summarizing 1934 communications regarding alleged patent violations in Japan affecting Pridwin Industries Company.
subfiles.summary: This docket sheet indexes two entries from April and June 1934 regarding alleged infringements of Pridwin Industries Company's patent rights by Japanese concerns. It records a report by Consul General Arthur Garrels in Tokyo forwarding case correspondence and details on the export of the affected articles. A subsequent legal opinion by Assistant Legal Adviser Ward advised forwarding the Consul General's letter to the addressee despite departure from ordinary Departmental procedure, in view of developing circumstances.
subfiles.title: Department of State List of Papers: Protection of Patents of Pridwin Industries Company in Japan

subfiles.about: Docket sheet recording 1934 interdepartmental coordination regarding patent and trademark infringements of Prophylactic Toothbrush Company products in Japan.
subfiles.summary: This docket sheet records communications from August 1934 concerning the infringement of Prophylactic Toothbrush Company's patents and trademarks by Japanese manufacturers. It details a conference between Eugene H. Dooman of the State Department's Division of Far Eastern Affairs and James L. Brown of the Department of Commerce, cross-referenced to the trademark decimal file. Additionally, it notes the receipt of correspondence and physical exhibits of infringing packages and labels transmitted by the Commerce Department to determine the most effective course of action.
subfiles.title: Department of State List of Papers: Infringement of Patents of the Prophylactic Toothbrush Company by Japanese Manufacturers

subfiles.about: Docket sheet summarizing the 1935 case regarding the copying and importation of A. Sauer and Company's patented tubular watch straps.
subfiles.summary: This docket sheet records four communications from July to September 1935 concerning duplicate tubular watch straps manufactured in Japan at low prices, initiated by Senator Vic Donahey on behalf of A. Sauer and Company of Cincinnati. While the Department initially offered to make diplomatic representations if Japanese patent laws were breached, patent attorney Joseph A. Rave clarified that the company sought solely to halt the importation of Japanese goods into the United States rather than stop manufacturing abroad. The Department responded that no diplomatic action was viable against goods legal under Japanese law, suggesting that the firm pursue federal court injunctions or petition the Secretary of the Treasury to exclude the infringing articles.
subfiles.title: Department of State List of Papers: Infringement of Patents of A. Sauer and Company by Japanese Manufacturers

subfiles.about: Docket sheet recording complaints, international investigations, and wartime economic restrictions involving Singer sewing machine patents, trademarks, and Japanese branch operations from 1934 to 1939.
subfiles.summary: This docket sheet outlines eight entries from May 1934 to May 1939 concerning the Singer Manufacturing Company and its Japanese subsidiary. Early entries detail complaints that the Japanese Legation in Lisbon was actively distributing circulars from Charten and Company of Kobe advertising counterfeit parts bearing Singer's 'SIMANCO' trademark, prompting an inquiry and photostat evidence from U.S. Minister John K. Caldwell in Portugal. Subsequent entries from 1938 and 1939 detail the increasing operational difficulties of Singer's Japanese branch under wartime import bans and exchange controls, concluding with a conference between Vice President Milton C. Lightner and State Department Adviser Stanley K. Hornbeck regarding blocked yen remittances.
subfiles.title: Department of State List of Papers: Infringement of Singer Manufacturing Company's Patent by Japanese
